::: {.callout-note}
## Recommendation

Use **five focused computational investigations plus one staged team project**. A1–A3 are individual; A4–A5 are completed in pairs with a short individual interpretation. This gives each major topic a roughly two-week assessment cycle without creating five full sets of individual marking. The recommended partition is **20% assignments + 20% project + 20% midterm + 40% final**. Exact due dates still require confirmation.
:::

## Evidence from Fall 2025

The available Fall 2025 archive contains:

- **seven conventional assignment briefs**, A1–A7, due from September 15 to November 17;
- **one team-project brief**, numbered A9 and due December 8;
- no A8 brief in the available archive, so it is not safe to infer its content;
- a syllabus that groups all assignments under **25%**, with a 30% midterm and 45% final.

The seven archived assignments progress through binary representation/Python, roots, nonlinear and linear systems, regression/interpolation, differentiation, and integration. The A9 project asks teams of five or six to run a common LAMMPS Cu study of melting, RDF, MSD, diffusivity, and Arrhenius fitting. Three hands-on decks introduce remote access, Linux/vi, and LAMMPS late in November.

Useful features to preserve are repeated computational practice, access to seminar starter code, and a real simulation study. Features to change are repetitive hand iteration, generic non-materials contexts, a large final-week team task, and insufficiently visible project milestones and individual accountability.

## Public U of A benchmark

A comprehensive current public archive of CME undergraduate syllabi could not be located, so this is a **small benchmark, not a departmental rule or census**.

| Public source | Assessment pattern | What it tells us |
|---|---|---|
| [CH E 318 Mass Transfer, Winter 2026](https://tiangroup-uofa.github.io/che318-mass-transfer/lectures/L01/) | Eight assignments, best seven counted: 25%; midterm: 30%; final: 45%; no project | Frequent assignments fit a conventional exam-centred course, but are not a good workload comparator once a substantial project is added. |
| [ENGG 404, Spring 2024 syllabus](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/engineering/media-library/school-engineering-safety-and-risk-management/program/engg404-2024s-course-syllabus-v20240502.pdf) | Four assignments plus quizzes: 21%; staged team project and surveys: 39%; final: 40%; no midterm | A project-heavy engineering course reduces the number of conventional assignments and gives the project an explicit category. |
| [ENGG 406, Winter 2023 syllabus](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/engineering/media-library/school-engineering-safety-and-risk-management/program/engg406-2023w-course-syllabus.pdf) | Quizzes: 10%; assignments: 30%; participation: 10%; final: 50%; no project or midterm | U of A engineering courses use materially different partitions; 25/30/45 is not a universal Faculty formula. |
| [UAPPOL Assessment and Grading Policy](https://www.ualberta.ca/en/alfresco/uappol/academic/assessment-and-grading/policy/assessment-and-grading-policy.pdf) | No prescribed number of assignments or fixed percentage split | Assessment should be aligned, clearly communicated, multifaceted, timely, and both formative and summative. Innovative forms are permitted. |

The [official MAT E 374 catalogue entry](https://apps.ualberta.ca/catalogue/course/mat_e/374) confirms that this is a 3-1S-0 course, but does not prescribe an assessment partition. The public evidence therefore supports using professional judgment and explicit alignment rather than copying seven or eight assignments from a course without a project.

For roughly 26 students, five fully individual assignments would mean **130 submissions**. The proposed three-individual plus two-pair pattern produces about **104 assignment artifacts**—the same marking count as four fully individual assignments and 43% fewer than seven individual assignments—before project marking.

## Proposed assignment set

| Assignment | Timing window | Main course units | Driving question | Required credibility evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A1 · Trust a computational result** | Weeks 2–3 | Orientation and Unit 1 | Which reported materials result is believable, and what error source limits it? | units/scale check, limiting or reference case, and an error/convergence plot |
| **A2 · Find a preferred state** | Weeks 4–5 | Unit 2 | Which equilibrium or relaxed state should be reported when roots, minima, and initial guesses compete? | bracket or landscape evidence, residual/gradient, sensitivity, and physical state classification |
| **A3 · Learn from sparse materials data** | Weeks 6–7 | Unit 3 | What parameter or prediction is supported by noisy, sparse data? | residuals, uncertainty/sensitivity, and an interpolation/extrapolation or validation check |
| **A4 · Predict materials evolution** *(pair)* | Weeks 8–9 | Unit 4 | Which kinetic prediction remains credible when timestep, tolerance, or mechanism changes? | timestep/tolerance refinement, reference/limit comparison, and individual interpretation of solver versus model error |
| **A5 · Conserve transport across a material** *(pair)* | Weeks 10–12 | Unit 5 | How do grid, boundary, timestep, and interface choices affect a diffusion or heat prediction? | conservation balance, mesh/timestep check, and individual materials conclusion |

Unit 6 sampling/MD and Unit 7 structure–energy content arrive too late for another large assignment. They should contribute to project synthesis, seminar evidence, and/or the final assessment.

## Working rhythm

| Assignment | Provisional due date | Submission mode |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Fri Sep 25 | individual |
| A2 | Fri Oct 9 | individual |
| A3 | Fri Oct 23 | individual |
| A4 | Fri Nov 6 | pair notebook + individual interpretation |
| A5 | Fri Nov 20 | pair notebook + individual interpretation |

A4 should be released early enough that the October 28 midterm does not consume its working period. A5 spans instructional time before and after Reading Week; no work should be expected during the break. No assignment is due after November 20, preserving three active project weeks through December 7.

## Common submission form

Each assignment should be a focused marimo investigation, normally completable in about **2–3 hours per student**, submitted as:

1. an executable marimo `.py` notebook or approved exported artifact;
2. a concise static HTML/PDF view for reliable grading and accessibility;
3. a short engineering conclusion embedded in the notebook—not a separate long report;
4. for A4–A5, clearly identified individual interpretation cells from both partners.

Every assignment must show:

1. **question and model**;
2. **assumptions, scales, units, and data provenance**;
3. **method choice** and why it fits;
4. **verification or uncertainty evidence**;
5. **physical interpretation**;
6. **limitations and reproducibility information**.

## Common rubric

| Criterion | Suggested share |
|---|---:|
| Formulation, assumptions, units, and scale | 20% |
| Numerical representation and method choice | 20% |
| Correct, reproducible computation | 20% |
| Verification, convergence, conservation, or uncertainty evidence | 25% |
| Materials interpretation and limitations | 15% |

This intentionally gives more weight to credibility and engineering judgment than to reproducing an algorithm from memory. A student should inspect or implement each central mechanism once; later work may use established library routines with appropriate diagnostics.

## Relationship to seminars

Seminars are the rehearsal space, not twelve extra assignments. Each graded investigation should build on one or two seminar patterns while changing the materials case, data, or decision. Students may reuse general seminar code, but the assessed verification and interpretation must be their own.

Recommended workflow:

- release after the relevant first seminar;
- include one assignment-specific clinic in the next seminar;
- allow roughly 10–14 days;
- avoid a due date during Reading Week, on the midterm date, or in the same final week as the project;
- publish the rubric and a static fallback with the brief.

## Recommended partition

| Component | Weight | Workload control |
|---|---:|---|
| Five investigations | 20% | 4% each; A1–A3 individual, A4–A5 paired |
| Staged team project | 20% | small proposal/checkpoint plus one final group artifact and individual reflection |
| Midterm | 20% | one focused 50-minute in-class assessment |
| Final examination | 40% | remains the largest individual summative assessment |

The lower midterm weight should make it **lower stakes, not artificially easy**. It should sample the essential pre-midterm outcomes with fewer time-pressure traps and provide useful feedback before the final. The three individual assignments, individual portions of paired work and the project, and examinations preserve enough individual evidence for grading confidence. Do not finalize due dates until the registered seminar day and official constraints are confirmed.
